note: Hand-curated updates on cryptology, intelligence, and quantum: cryptography and post-quantum migration, cryptanalysis, signals intelligence, steganography and covert channels, and quantum computing. Public sources only. Each entry separates sourced reporting from assessment and ends with the debate, presenting competing positions as their holders argue them. Entries do not assess the status of any specific U.S. system.

entries.title: NASA's First U.S. Air-to-Ground Quantum Link: A Milestone With the Numbers Withheld
entries.bottomLine: NASA locked onto a quantum signal from an aircraft in flight on October 21, a first for the U.S. but not for the world, and it has released no performance data. The larger question is whether quantum links will ever protect national security traffic. NSA's current answer is no.
requires: On October 21, 2026, NASA Glenn researchers sent photons over a quantum channel between a Pilatus PC-12 and a ground station, locking onto the signal and recording data in flight. NASA describes this as the first such link in the U.S.
NASA frames the test as a first step toward aircraft operating inside wider quantum networks.
Not disclosed: link distance, photon rate, error rate, key rate, or whether keys were generated or photons entangled.
Earlier airborne quantum links abroad: a German air-to-ground QKD demonstration published in 2013, and a Canadian flight in 2016 that received quantum signals sent up to an aircraft.
On October 1, 2026, NSA reissued its position: it does not recommend quantum cryptography, including QKD, to protect national security systems unless several technical limitations are overcome.

keyDates.label: NSA reissues its position on quantum cryptography and QKD for NSS
NASA Glenn air-to-ground quantum link test flight
NASA announces the result

strategicRead.head: A U.S. first, not a world first.
strategicRead.body: German and Canadian teams flew airborne quantum links years earlier, and China demonstrated satellite-to-ground QKD in 2017. The significance is U.S. government capability-building in free-space quantum links, not novelty.

strategicRead.head: The headline outruns the data.
strategicRead.body: Without a key rate, error rate, or distance, nothing about operational usefulness can be assessed. Viral reposts compounded this: at least one widely shared post dropped NASA's own 'in the U.S.' qualifier and called it a first-ever.

strategicRead.head: Two agencies, two bets, no contradiction.
strategicRead.body: NASA is investing in quantum networking for science and space communications. NSA's position is that post-quantum algorithms, not QKD, protect national security systems. These are different missions, but coverage describing this test as 'unbreakable' secure communications does not match the stated position of the agency that sets U.S. national security cryptography.

indicators: NASA publishing distance, error rate, or key rate for the October flight
Follow-on flights at longer range, or with entangled photons
Any public DoD or AFRL airborne quantum communication program
Revisions to NSA's QKD position or the CNSA 2.0 FAQ
New Chinese quantum satellite or airborne milestones

debate.intro: The test reopens an old split: whether quantum key distribution has any role in national security, or whether post-quantum algorithms make it unnecessary.

positions.axis: Does QKD have a national security future?
positions.position: PQC is the answer; QKD adds cost and risk
positions.heldBy: NSA; several European national cybersecurity agencies have published similar reservations
positions.argument: QKD only authenticates with help from classical cryptography, needs specialized hardware and trusted relay nodes, and is hard to validate in the field. Post-quantum algorithms run on existing networks and can be standardized, tested, and certified.
positions.confidence: High

positions.axis: Does QKD have a national security future?
positions.position: Physics-based security is a hedge worth building
positions.heldBy: QKD researchers and vendors; programs such as the EU's EuroQCI; China's state investment
positions.argument: Post-quantum algorithms rest on mathematical assumptions that are not proven and could fall to a breakthrough. QKD's security rests on physics. Layering both hedges against the failure of either.
positions.confidence: Medium

debate.synthesis: Neither side disputes the engineering limits. The disagreement is over how much to pay now as insurance against a future mathematical break.
debate.openQuestion: If post-quantum algorithms ever fall to a mathematical breakthrough rather than a quantum computer, will the countries that built quantum networks hold the advantage, or will QKD's practical limits make the investment moot?

updates.text: NEC and IBM Japan demonstrated hybrid TLS that combines a QKD key (ETSI GS QKD 014 interface) with ML-KEM-768 through HKDF, with ML-DSA-44 for authentication. Validation ran July–September. No performance figures published (company-reported, via The Quantum Insider).

At SC26, a consortium showed an '8,000 km' Chicago–Amsterdam–Bilbao quantum-safe link. Hype check: QKD (Luxquanta CV-QKD) ran only on links under 1 km at the Chicago show floor and 25 km in Bilbao. The ~1,200 km and ~7,000 km legs, including the ocean crossing, used ML-KEM post-quantum cryptography, with Ciena optical encryption. Self-reported by the consortium.

entries.title: CNSA 2.0: NSA's Post-Quantum Deadlines for National Security Systems
entries.bottomLine: The decisive date is not 2035. It is January 1, 2027, when new national security system acquisitions are supposed to be CNSA 2.0 compliant. From that point, the quantum transition is decided in contracts more than in labs.
requires: One algorithm set at every classification level: ML-KEM-1024 for key establishment, ML-DSA-87 for signatures, AES-256, SHA-384/512, and LMS or XMSS hash-based signatures for software and firmware signing.

No hybrid requirement. NSA says it will not require hybrid certified products, and directs that hybrid or non-standardized quantum-resistant solutions not be used on NSS mission systems except where NSA recommends them.

Software and firmware signing moves first. NSA's stated reason: validation algorithms are often locked in for a system's life, so a quantum-resistant root of trust may be needed years before the rest of the system is upgraded.
Signing sources that are themselves national security systems must use CMVP-validated hardware. NSA states no waivers will be granted for this.

Until Commercial Solutions for Classified (CSfC) capability packages support CNSA 2.0, NSA allows pre-shared symmetric keys as a near-term option, which it rates above unvalidated post-quantum public-key algorithms.

NSM-10: NSS agencies adopt symmetric-key protections for quantum-vulnerable key exchanges, where appropriate

End of the grace period for systems validated under NIAP or CSfC profiles
NSPM-12 re-establishes CNSS and lets it issue binding directives to NSS owners
EO 14412: federal high-value systems must use PQC key establishment by end of 2030, signatures by end of 2031
NSA PQC measures under EO 14412; PQC Resource Hub launched
NIST IR 8547 final: all RSA and elliptic-curve public-key algorithms deprecated after 2030, disallowed after 2035
New NSS acquisitions must be CNSA 2.0 compliant, unless otherwise noted
Equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 phased out
CNSA 2.0 algorithms mandated, unless otherwise noted
Goal: all national security systems quantum-resistant (NSM-10)

strategicRead.head: The acquisition date is the real deadline.
strategicRead.body: The 2035 goal gets the headlines, but the January 2027 acquisition rule does more of the work. Military platforms and their communications equipment stay in service for decades, so equipment bought in 2026 under the older CNSA 1.0 suite can still be fielded long after 2035. The 2030 phase-out date exists to deal with that tail. In practice, the transition for national security systems is being decided in procurement offices and vendor roadmaps, years before anyone knows whether a cryptographically relevant quantum computer will exist.
strategicRead.confidence: High on the dates · Medium on the assessment

strategicRead.head: The sequence follows asset lifetime, not threat timing.
strategicRead.body: Two different clocks are running. For confidentiality, the clock is harvest-now-decrypt-later: traffic recorded today is exposed the day a capable quantum computer exists, so key establishment is urgent for anything that must stay secret for decades. For integrity, the clock is immutability: a signing key locked into fielded hardware cannot be swapped once forgery becomes possible. Moving hash-based firmware signing first is NSA's answer to the second clock. Most public commentary only discusses the first.
strategicRead.confidence: High — NSA's stated rationale and the standard harvest-now model

strategicRead.head: One parameter set for everything is a deliberate trade.
strategicRead.body: NSA chose the largest parameter sets at every classification level instead of scaling strength to sensitivity. That buys margin and simplicity and charges it to bandwidth and processing. An ML-DSA-87 signature is 4,627 bytes; an ECDSA P-256 signature is 64, roughly 72 times smaller. On fiber that is a rounding error. On constrained tactical links, satellite channels, and small embedded devices it is an engineering problem, and it lands on the systems least able to absorb it.
strategicRead.confidence: High on sizes · Medium on where the burden concentrates

strategicRead.head: Allies are not making the same bet.
strategicRead.body: NSA does not require hybrid schemes and steers national security systems away from them, citing added complexity, interoperability burden, and a second migration later. France's ANSSI takes the opposite position and recommends hybrid mechanisms that pair a classical algorithm with a post-quantum one; Germany's BSI is reported to recommend the same. Neither position is careless. They price different risks: NSA treats complexity and a second transition as the larger danger, while ANSSI treats an undiscovered weakness in young lattice-based mathematics as the larger danger and keeps a classical layer as insurance. The practical cost falls on coalition communications, where U.S. and European equipment has to agree on a common mode.
strategicRead.confidence: High on NSA and ANSSI positions · Medium on BSI (secondhand) · Medium on interoperability friction

indicators: NIAP protection profiles and CSfC capability packages adding CNSA 2.0 support ahead of the January 2027 acquisition rule.
Vendor announcements of CNSA 2.0-validated products, especially networking and embedded equipment, where larger keys and signatures cost the most.
Any published cryptanalytic result that weakens ML-KEM or ML-DSA. That is the single event that would vindicate the hybrid approach.
Whether NATO or Five Eyes guidance converges on hybrid or pure post-quantum for coalition links.
Further revisions to NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ, which NSA has already updated since 2022.
New documents on NSA's PQC Resource Hub, especially any CSfC capability package supporting CNSA 2.0
Public DoD or Navy statements on how cryptographic upgrades are scheduled into shortened ship maintenance periods.

debate.intro: Experts argue about this on two separate axes: how to migrate, and how urgent it is.

positions.heldBy: NSA; Australia's ASD (reported)
positions.argument: The new algorithms are trusted. Pairing them with classical algorithms adds complexity and interoperability burden, and guarantees a second migration later to remove the classical half.
positions.confidence: High — NSA's stated position

positions.position: Keep a classical layer as insurance
positions.heldBy: France's ANSSI; Germany's BSI (reported)
positions.argument: Post-quantum math is young, and it has already failed once in public. In July 2022, SIKE, a fourth-round candidate in NIST's competition, was broken by two researchers at KU Leuven using a single classical CPU core in about an hour. A hybrid scheme fails only if both layers fail.
positions.confidence: High on positions and the SIKE break

positions.heldBy: Peter Gutmann, University of Auckland, and other skeptics
positions.argument: No quantum computer has factored a number larger than 21 without tricks, and publicized records have used specially chosen numbers that classical methods also crack. On this view, migration is expensive, the new algorithms are less efficient, and the effort distracts from the failures actually behind most breaches.
positions.confidence: High that this is his position · disputed by researchers including Daniel Bernstein and Scott Aaronson

positions.heldBy: Resource-estimate research, including Google Quantum AI
positions.argument: In 2019 the estimate to break RSA-2048 was about 20 million noisy qubits. In May 2025 Craig Gidney of Google Quantum AI put it under 1 million, in under a week. A February 2026 simulation-only result claimed under 100,000. In October 2026 Alice & Bob estimated about 23,000 of its cat qubits, under optimistic hardware assumptions. No machine is near these numbers, but the target keeps moving toward the hardware, and harvest-now-decrypt-later means the exposure starts when data is collected.
positions.confidence: High on the published estimates · the 2026 result is simulation only

debate.synthesis: The skeptic and the urgent case can both be right: no machine today is close, and the machine required keeps getting smaller. Planning happens in that gap.
debate.openQuestion: Is 2035 set by the threat or by capacity? NSM-10's wording is "mitigating as much of the quantum risk as is feasible by 2035." That phrasing concedes the goal is bounded by how fast the government can migrate, not by any forecast of quantum progress. If a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives earlier than expected, the binding constraint will not be the algorithms, which already exist. It will be acquisition speed, and the equipment bought before January 2027.

updates.text: NSA announced new post-quantum measures under Executive Order 14412 and launched a Post-Quantum Cryptography Resource Hub. The release restates the CNSSP 15 milestones (new commercial NSS support quantum-resistant algorithms from 2027; legacy systems that cannot are phased out by 2030) and changes no deadline. The same day, NSA reissued its position that quantum key distribution is not recommended for NSS.

Alice & Bob, a French quantum hardware company, published a preprint estimating that about 22,593 of its 'cat qubits' could break RSA-2048 in 3.14 days, and that under 30,000 could break the elliptic-curve keys used by Bitcoin in about an hour. That is far below Gidney's 2025 estimate of under 1 million qubits. Caveats: the paper is not peer reviewed, and it was written by the company that builds the hardware. Its headline figure assumes qubits that essentially never suffer bit-flip errors (about 100 years); with bit-flip times of about one hour, the estimate roughly doubles to about 45,000 qubits. The company has reported bit-flip times of 44 minutes on a single cat qubit (2025) and 189 to 252 minutes on its 12-qubit Helium 2 processor (November 2026, company-reported). The larger gap is scale: from 12 qubits to tens of thousands, while meeting the paper's other error-rate assumptions. Press headlines claiming encryption 'could fall in 3 days' describe a hypothetical machine, not one that exists. No deadline changes.

NIST finalized IR 8547, its plan for retiring quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography. All RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA, Diffie-Hellman and ECDH are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035 under NIST standards. The change from the 2024 draft: 128-bit algorithms such as P-256, which the draft let run to 2035 without a deprecation step, now follow the same 2030 date as 112-bit ones. This is the civilian counterpart to CNSA 2.0: NSS follow CNSSP 15's earlier 2027/2030/2031 dates, and federal high-value systems follow EO 14412's 2030/2031 dates. No CNSA 2.0 deadline changes.

At TechNet Indo-Pacific, Capt. Victor Taylor of Pacific Fleet said Navy maintenance windows have shrunk from roughly nine months to a year down to about 45 days (as reported by Defense One). The panel discussed this as a practical constraint on upgrading cryptography in fielded ships ahead of the 2030 and 2031 deadlines. This is a public remark about scheduling, not an assessment of any system's status.

GAO-27-108740 (issued Oct. 6, revised Oct. 14): none of the 24 CFO Act agencies fully met GAO's practices for cryptographic inventory, migration funding, and testing. 23 had tested no post-quantum algorithms, and 18 reported lacking cryptographic expertise. GAO made 89 recommendations, detailed in a sensitive version. No deadline changes.

NSA, Australia's ASD/ACSC, and CISA published 'Post-quantum questions to ask your vendors,' a five-phase guide from inventory to communication for procurement, renewals, and assurance. It is guidance and changes no deadline.

Federal buying signals: GSA issued an RFI on commercial PQC products and services for the federal migration (responses due Dec. 7; market research only). GSA's D. Pomeroy said post-quantum algorithms have been loaded onto PIV smart-card chips (CyberScoop; algorithms not named, no GSA primary yet). Commerce's Paul Dabbar said the department plans a PQC demonstration for companies in December (Federal News Network).

South Korea's NIS released draft cryptographic security standards and a PQC migration guidebook for public agencies (Digital Today). A key-management guideline is expected by end-2026 and final versions in H1 2027. Not yet confirmed on an NIS/NCSC primary page.

IOSCO report PD833: most securities firms and regulators are still at the inventory stage, and few are testing. It notes that Israel directed banks and licensed payment providers to prepare formal quantum-readiness plans, and it warns against 'quantum washing.' The view that firms should prepare for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer within five years is attributed to some industry participants, not to IOSCO.

entries.title: DARPA QBI Stage C: Testing Whether a Useful Quantum Computer Can Exist by 2033
entries.bottomLine: DARPA has moved four more quantum approaches into Stage C, where government evaluators test whether a utility-scale machine can actually be built. It is the closest thing to an independent, official clock on quantum progress, and the date it is testing is 2033.
requires: On October 7, 2026, DARPA advanced Atom Computing (neutral atoms), Diraq (silicon spin qubits), IBM (modular superconducting) and IonQ (trapped ions) to Stage C of the Quantum Benchmarking Initiative. Microsoft and PsiQuantum were already in Stage C through the earlier US2QC pilot.
QBI's question is whether any approach can reach utility-scale operation, defined as computational value exceeding cost, by 2033. DARPA frames it as a question, not a commitment.

Stage A is a short concept evaluation. Stage B is a yearlong review of R&D plans, technical risks and prototypes; 11 teams advanced to it in November 2025. Stage C is independent verification by a government test-and-evaluation team.

About $200 million in new DARPA funding covers the four entrants, against a Stage C ceiling of up to $300 million per performer over multiple years. Several Stage B teams were not selected, and DARPA expects further selections.

keyDates.label: QBI Stage B: 11 teams advance (reported)
QBI Stage C: Atom Computing, Diraq, IBM and IonQ advance
CNSA 2.0: new national security system acquisitions must comply
QBI target: utility-scale quantum operation
NSM-10 goal: national security systems quantum-resistant

strategicRead.head: An independent clock, not a vendor roadmap.
strategicRead.body: Most public quantum timelines come from companies raising capital. QBI is the first U.S. government effort to check those claims against engineering evidence, using its own evaluation team. A Stage C success would give the 2033 question a credible answer. Universal failure would be just as informative.
strategicRead.confidence: High on program design · Medium on significance

strategicRead.head: Utility is not the same as breaking RSA.
strategicRead.body: QBI measures whether a machine's value exceeds its cost. Chemistry or materials simulation could clear that bar long before a machine can run Shor's algorithm against RSA-2048, which the best published estimate (Gidney, Google Quantum AI, 2025) still places near one million noisy qubits. A Stage C success would shorten threat timelines without itself creating a cryptographically relevant quantum computer.

strategicRead.head: 2033 lands in the middle of the migration.
strategicRead.body: The QBI date falls after the CNSA 2.0 phase-out deadlines of 2030 and 2031 and two years before the 2035 NSM-10 goal. A verified utility-scale machine in 2033 would arrive while legacy equipment is still being retired, which makes the acquisition decisions of 2026 and 2027 the ones that count.

indicators: Further Stage C selections, and which Stage B teams leave the program.
Results published by the government evaluation team, as distinct from performer press releases.
Logical-qubit error rates reported against Stage C milestones.
Congressional action on the reported proposal to raise annual military quantum spending to about $567 million.

debate.intro: The argument is less about QBI itself than about what its answer would mean.

positions.position: A useful machine this decade is realistic
positions.heldBy: Stage C performers, including IBM and IonQ (company statements)
positions.argument: Each has published a roadmap to fault-tolerant systems within the decade, and selection for Stage C means those plans survived a year of government technical review.
positions.confidence: High that this is their position · roadmaps are unverified

positions.heldBy: Skeptics of quantum timelines in the research community
positions.argument: Past quantum milestones have often relied on problems chosen to favor quantum hardware. A machine that beats its cost on a narrow task may say little about general or cryptographic capability.
positions.confidence: Medium — a general skeptic position, not a published response to QBI

positions.position: Plan as if the answer is yes
positions.heldBy: NSA's CNSA 2.0 posture
positions.argument: Harvest-now-decrypt-later makes data collected today exposed whenever a capable machine appears, so migration timelines cannot wait for QBI's verdict.
positions.confidence: High — NSA's stated rationale

debate.synthesis: QBI cannot say when RSA breaks. It can replace company roadmaps with government-verified evidence on whether the hardware path is real.
debate.openQuestion: If a Stage C performer demonstrates utility-scale operation before 2033, does the 2035 migration goal move earlier, or does the government keep setting its deadline by how fast it can migrate rather than by the threat?

updates.text: DARPA's W. Mason said the first QBI Stage C engagements are planned for January (Federal News Network). No new performers named.

Commerce finalized a CHIPS R&D award of up to $100 million to Atom Computing, part of the May 21 letters of intent worth $2.01 billion, with minority equity stakes in seven quantum firms (NIST). Atom Computing, Diraq, and IBM in that group are also QBI Stage C performers. IBM separately said it will offer access to a dual-processor system ('Nighthawk r3') in 2027 (Ars Technica; company-reported).

NVIDIA, IBM, and Fermilab announced plans for a quantum-classical co-design platform that colocates NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including Nighthawk. Separately, NVIDIA released a CUDA-Q error-correction decoder (TCBP-JOBS) that it says is up to 13,000x faster than leading algorithms, cutting one design-study workload from 12 weeks to 45 minutes (about 2,700x). Hype check: this is classical GPU computing used to research error-correction designs, not a quantum computer solving a problem, and the figures are company-reported. Headlines calling it a 'quantum computing breakthrough' overstate it.

Alice & Bob updated its roadmap: 200 logical qubits by 2030 from about 3,600 cat qubits (previous target: 100), and a 2034 'Neon' system of 2,048 logical qubits aimed at RSA-2048 stress-testing. Company-reported, with no logical error rates given; results drawn from France's PROQCIMA program.

entries.title: Binance: $6.3 Billion Taken Without Breaking a Single Key
entries.bottomLine: Every signature in the largest digital-asset theft on record appears to have been cryptographically valid. The failure was in what the signing pipeline was told to authorize, which makes custody procedure, not cryptography, the attack surface.
requires: Binance disclosed the incident on October 29, 2026, putting affected assets at about $6.3 billion. Funds began leaving at 20:05 UTC; containment took until 00:10 UTC on October 30.

Access was built over months. Binance says a fake job interview in September led an engineer to install zero-day malware disguised as a coding test, and a tampered Homebrew package compromised another engineer in June. On October 20 attackers used an internal AI tool to reach two wallet engineers' machines.

The largest Ethereum loss used EIP-7702 delegation, which lets an ordinary account sign a standing delegation of its execution to contract code. Binance has not said how the authorizations were obtained.

About $2.85 billion has been frozen, per Binance. On October 31 the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, the unit it also blamed for the February 2025 Bybit theft. North Korea denies involvement.

keyDates.label: Bybit theft (about $1.5 billion), later attributed to TraderTraitor by the FBI
Attackers reach two wallet engineers' machines
Funds leave Binance; incident disclosed (about $6.3 billion)
FBI attributes theft to TraderTraitor and publishes addresses to block
Binance root-cause briefing; KCNA denial

strategicRead.head: Kerckhoffs held. The keyholder did not.
strategicRead.body: Modern custody assumes the adversary knows the system and protects the key with hardware security modules, multi-party computation and signing thresholds. Those controls decide who can sign. They do not decide what a signer is shown or why a signature is requested. DMM Bitcoin, Bybit and Binance were all lost at that layer.

strategicRead.head: The entry point was a person, again.
strategicRead.body: The fake-recruiter lure matches the pattern U.S. agencies have described for TraderTraitor since 2022. The cryptographic controls held; the intrusion ran through hiring-style social engineering and a developer's toolchain. That is a counterintelligence problem as much as a security-engineering one.
strategicRead.confidence: High (pattern) · Medium (applies to this case per Binance's account)

strategicRead.head: EIP-7702 changes what one signature is worth.
strategicRead.body: A single valid delegation can confer standing control of an account rather than approve one transfer. That raises the payoff of compromising the signing pipeline once, and staged authorizations imply the attacker held signing capability well before the cash-out.
strategicRead.confidence: Medium — Binance has not disclosed how the authorizations were obtained

strategicRead.head: A sanctions problem as much as a cyber problem.
strategicRead.body: Stolen digital assets are a significant revenue source for a sanctioned nuclear-armed state. Freezing about $2.85 billion is unusually large, but roughly $2.4 billion in ETH and BTC remains outside reach, which makes the laundering phase the next point of contest.

indicators: OFAC designations or DOJ forfeiture actions tied to the laundering addresses
Movement of the unfrozen ETH and BTC through bridges, mixers and OTC brokers
Binance's independent review and any disclosure of how the EIP-7702 authorizations were obtained
Wallet or client changes in the Ethereum ecosystem that limit standing delegations
Copycat fake-recruiter campaigns against other exchanges' engineers

updates.text: Binance briefing: initial access began in September with a fake job interview that led an engineer to run a malware-laced 'coding assignment' on a work computer; a tampered Homebrew package compromised another engineer in June. Attackers reached wallet engineers on October 20 and moved funds on October 29. About $2.85 billion frozen; Binance says it replenished roughly 98% of affected tokens from company funds.
North Korea denied involvement. KCNA carried a statement from Kim Yo Jong calling the FBI claim 'absurd rhetoric' and a 'grave political provocation.'

FBI attributed the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor, said the assets were mostly converted to Ethereum and would be further laundered, and published addresses for exchanges to block. No technical evidence was released with the notice.

DOJ (PR 26-1356): of more than $6 billion stolen, over $2.7 billion has been frozen and the department obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion. It describes the actors as members of the North Korean military that the FBI calls TraderTraitor. Tracing continues; no charges were announced.

Same release, separate scheme: 'FaceStealer,' more than $400 million stolen over 18 months. Attackers invite targets to video calls from hijacked accounts, play recorded or deepfaked video of known contacts, fake a technical problem, and push a 'fix' that installs malware. Targets include crypto and Web3 workers and open-source maintainers, which the FBI says suggests supply-chain aims. The Central District of California disrupted the infrastructure, and the FBI seized more than 900 victim webcam videos. Aliases listed include Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, BlueNoroff, and APT38.

Google's GTIG described a suspected DPRK cluster (MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE) that reached crypto firms through fake recruiter profiles, then edited Claude Code settings files in internal repositories so the tool downloaded a backdoor. This is the same recruiter-lure entry point as the Binance theft, now using AI developer tooling. See ai-001.

A Threat Disruption Center launched for the Homeland Security Task Force (30+ federal agencies, 440+ state and local), with TRM Labs on a roughly $95 million one-year non-competed deal (Bloomberg via Claims Journal). Reported FBI figure: about $21 billion in cybercrime losses last year, more than half involving crypto. No DHS or White House primary yet.

debate.intro: With the cryptography intact and the attribution public, the argument is over where the fix belongs.

positions.heldBy: Custody security practitioners; exchange security teams
positions.argument: Each recent mega-theft ran through a compromised employee device. The priority is endpoint isolation for signing staff, out-of-band verification of what a transaction does, and treating recruiter contact as a threat vector.
positions.confidence: High

positions.heldBy: Critics of EIP-7702's design among Ethereum security researchers
positions.argument: A single signature that grants standing control raises the value of one compromise. Wallets and clients should limit, scope, or expire delegations so that a stolen signature buys less.
positions.confidence: Medium

positions.heldBy: U.S. sanctions and law-enforcement approach (FBI, Treasury)
positions.argument: Defenders cannot out-patch a state program indefinitely. Attribution, published addresses, sanctions on laundering services and asset seizures raise the cost of cashing out, which is where the revenue is realized.
positions.confidence: Medium

debate.synthesis: The three positions are not exclusive. The disagreement is over which layer gets priority spending, and whether thefts at this scale are private security failures or a national security problem.
debate.openQuestion: If the math held and the people failed, is a $6 billion theft by a sanctioned state a cybersecurity failure or a counter-proliferation failure, and which institution should be accountable for stopping the next one?

entries.title: Fitburg Verdict: Finland Convicts a Crew for Cutting Baltic Cables, and Stops at the Crew
entries.bottomLine: A Helsinki court ruled that dragging an anchor about 130 km across the Gulf of Finland seabed was deliberate sabotage and jailed the ship's captain and boatswain. It is the first conviction in Finland's two anchor-dragging trials. It does not answer who, if anyone, wanted the cables cut: no government has publicly attributed the incident to the Russian state.
requires: On November 5, 2026, three judges of the Helsinki District Court unanimously convicted captain Andrei Maksimenko (57, Russian) and boatswain Vusal Majidov (48, Azerbaijani) of aggravated sabotage. Sentences: 3 years 6 months and 2 years 10 months, unconditional, with immediate detention.
A second count, aggravated interference with telecommunications, was dismissed because the sabotage conviction already covers it.
Damages: about €1.9 million jointly, plus €85,000 from the captain alone.

The court found the anchor chain and anchor were dragged about 130 km over several hours, that both men must have known, and that the acts were intentional. Prosecutors did not allege the captain ordered the anchor lowered; the court held both responsible for letting the voyage continue, and found the boatswain helped the dragging continue for about two hours after Finnish authorities contacted the crew.
The damage occurred outside Finnish territorial waters. The court claimed jurisdiction because the effects were felt in Finland.
The ship: Fitburg, a 132 m general cargo vessel flagged in St. Vincent and the Grenadines, owned and operated by a Turkish company, en route from St. Petersburg to Haifa.

On December 31, 2025, Elisa's Helsinki–Tallinn data cable failed (noticed at 04:53 local time) and Arelion reported an interruption on a second Finland–Estonia cable. The anchor also crossed seven other cables and a gas pipeline, which the court said were put at risk.

The Finnish Border Guard seized the ship around 11:00 the same day. Finnish Customs found EU-sanctioned Russian steel aboard but dropped the sanctions case because the ship had entered Finnish waters at the authorities' request. The ship was released January 12, 2026; charges were filed June 15, 2026.
Both men denied the charges. The ruling is not final; the captain's lawyer says he will appeal.

strategicRead.head: The legal path is being built case by case.
strategicRead.body: In October 2025 the same court dismissed the Eagle S case, ruling that under the law of the sea the flag state, not Finland, had jurisdiction. In August 2026 the Court of Appeal reversed that. Now the Fitburg court has convicted on the basis that the effects were felt in Finland. Together these rulings point toward a workable route for prosecuting damage outside territorial waters. Whether it holds depends on the appeals.
strategicRead.confidence: High on the rulings · Medium on where the case law settles

strategicRead.head: Intent is proven. Sponsorship is not.
strategicRead.body: The court established that the crew acted deliberately. It did not, and was not asked to, establish why. In January 2026 Finland's security intelligence service, Supo, said it takes no position on Fitburg and sees no sign of Russia preparing intermediaries for sabotage at sea. The Defence Forces' intelligence chief said no direct Russian link had been established, though on the broader pattern of incidents 'we believe a state actor is behind it.' That gap between a proven act and an unproven sponsor is the analytically important part of the story.
strategicRead.confidence: High that these are the officials' stated positions

strategicRead.head: Layered ownership slows everything down.
strategicRead.body: A Caribbean flag, a Turkish owner, a Russian captain, an Azerbaijani boatswain, sanctioned Russian cargo, and an Israeli destination. Earlier cases look similar: Eagle S was Cook Islands-flagged, NewNew Polar Bear Hong Kong-flagged. Whether or not that structure is deliberate, it spreads legal responsibility across several states and makes both attribution and enforcement slow.
strategicRead.confidence: High on the facts · Medium on the assessment

strategicRead.head: Detection and seizure are getting faster.
strategicRead.body: The first cable fault was noticed at 04:53 and the ship was seized around 11:00 the same morning. Charges followed in under six months and a verdict in just over ten. The Border Guard also mapped the drag trail on the seabed, which became evidence. Fast physical response is the part of the problem states can already control.

indicators: The captain's appeal, and whether the Court of Appeal accepts the 'effects in Finland' basis for jurisdiction.
The Eagle S retrial on the merits, and whether a Supreme Court appeal was filed.
Any official attribution of the Fitburg incident by Finland, Estonia, the EU, or NATO.
New legal tools for boarding or inspecting ships in exclusive economic zones.
Further Baltic incidents, and how quickly Baltic Sentry patrols detect them.

debate.intro: The verdict settles what happened on the ship. Two arguments remain open: what it proves, and what actually deters the next incident.

positions.heldBy: Pekka Turunen, Finnish Defence Forces intelligence chief (on the broader pattern, not Fitburg specifically)
positions.argument: Taken one at a time, each incident can be explained as negligence or crew misconduct. Taken together, the repetition suggests a state actor, even without a direct link in any single case.
positions.confidence: Medium: his remark concerned the pattern, not this case

positions.heldBy: Supo (Finnish Security Intelligence Service), January 2026; the defendants deny the charges
positions.argument: A court can establish that a crew acted deliberately. It cannot, on that evidence alone, establish who benefited. Supo publicly declined to attribute Fitburg and said it saw no sign of Russia preparing intermediaries.
positions.confidence: High that this is Supo's stated position

positions.heldBy: Finnish prosecutors and courts
positions.argument: Prison sentences and damages put a real cost on the people aboard and the companies behind them, and each conviction strengthens the legal route for the next case.
positions.confidence: High on the approach · its deterrent effect is untested

positions.heldBy: NATO, through Baltic Sentry (launched January 2025)
positions.argument: Courts act months after the damage. A visible naval and surveillance presence aims to deter incidents, or catch them as they happen.
positions.confidence: High on the stated aim · effectiveness not publicly measured

debate.synthesis: Both responses now run in parallel. The criminal case answers who was responsible on board; it was never designed to answer who, if anyone, wanted the outcome.
debate.openQuestion: If a sponsor is never proven, is convicting the crew the ceiling of the response? One view holds that treating each incident as a separate crime is the only fair standard, because states should not be accused without evidence. The other holds that case-by-case prosecution lets a campaign, if one exists, hide inside a series of ordinary-looking accidents. Which risk is worse for a democracy: wrongly blaming a state, or never being able to name one?

The consultation closes Jan. 14, 2027. This addresses the gap Fitburg exposed, where liability stopped at the crew.

The Royal Navy announced a £90 million 'Atlantic Net' framework with Ocean Infinity for drones and sensors to protect undersea cables and hunt submarines (Naval News; Sea Power Conference, Oslo). No gov.uk primary found yet.

Pakistan's PTA reported an SMW5 cable fault about 11 km offshore; traffic was rerouted, and NetBlocks and Cloudflare showed national HTTP traffic down as much as 36%. On Nov. 21 Transworld told customers it aims to finish repairs by Dec. 6 (Dawn). The cause has not been stated, and no one has claimed sabotage. Claims online linking it to the IRGC or Hormuz are unsupported.

entries.title: GPS Went Dark Over New Mexico: A Fatal Crash and the Case for Navigation Without Satellites
entries.bottomLine: The NTSB's preliminary report on the May 14 air ambulance crash near Ruidoso records the crew losing GPS during a scheduled military jamming window. It does not find a cause. For this track the case matters because it is a fully public, domestic record of what losing GPS does to ordinary navigation, which is the problem quantum navigation is being funded to solve.
requires: The crash: a Beech C90 (N249CP) operated by Generations Jets as a Part 135 air ambulance crashed about 00:15 local on May 14, 2026, near Lincoln, New Mexico, at about 9,950 ft in the Capitan Mountains. Both pilots and both flight nurses were killed (NTSB WPR26FA186, preliminary).

About 8 minutes after leaving Roswell, the pilot told Albuquerque Center they had lost GPS and asked for the ILS approach instead. A controller called a supervisor to ask the military to stop jamming. About 00:10, after the crew reported Ruidoso in sight and was cleared for a visual approach, the supervisor told the military it could resume. Impact followed about 5 minutes later.
Three other aircraft reported losing GPS that night. One had trouble identifying a ground-based navigation beacon and needed extra help from controllers.
A NOTAM warned that GPS 'MAY NOT BE AVBL' within 366 nautical miles of a point near White Sands Missile Range during the test window.

The report also records a dark night (0% moon), an out-of-service weather station at the destination, approach charts that are not authorized without a local altimeter setting, and terrain rising to 10,201 ft between the aircraft and the airport. The NTSB has not determined a probable cause or contributing factors.

On November 6, the GPS Innovation Alliance's Lisa Dyer said military jamming and spoofing tests are expanding outside conflict zones, that some ran without NOTAMs, and urged a larger test range (DefenseScoop). The Pentagon did not comment; the Army said the incident is under investigation.
The FCC is separately considering letting officials jam and spoof near correctional facilities, to counter contraband drones and phones (DefenseScoop).

keyDates.label: UK flies quantum inertial navigation on a test aircraft (Infleqtion UK, BAE Systems, QinetiQ)
C-17 flies with quantum magnetic navigation as its primary navigation method (SandboxAQ, JB Charleston)
DIU Transition of Quantum Sensing: 18 companies, more than 10 field tests planned
DARPA Robust Quantum Sensors awards to Q-CTRL ($24.4M across two contracts)

strategicRead.head: A rare public record of GPS denial.
strategicRead.body: Most reporting on jamming comes from conflict zones and relies on aggregate maps. Here there is a minute-by-minute federal timeline: four aircraft affected, controllers asking a test range to pause, a crew switching to ground-based approaches. It shows the practical effect of GPS denial in plain terms: workload rises and crews fall back on older systems.

strategicRead.head: It does not show cause, and should not be written as if it does.
strategicRead.body: The NTSB's preliminary report lists GPS loss alongside other conditions: a moonless night, a visual approach toward mountains, and no local altimeter setting. Jamming had been paused for about five minutes and resumed about five minutes before impact. Whether GPS loss contributed is the question the final report has to answer.
strategicRead.confidence: High on the record · no assessment of cause

strategicRead.head: Why it belongs on a quantum tab.
strategicRead.body: Quantum sensors are being funded as a GPS-independent backup: atom-based inertial sensors that drift less, and magnetometers and gravimeters that match readings to maps. DIU and DARPA are paying for field trials now. For civil aviation the near-term answers are procedural (better test coordination and notice) and conventional backups. Quantum navigation is a longer bet, and most performance figures published so far are company-reported.
strategicRead.confidence: High on the programs · Medium on the assessment

indicators: The NTSB final report and probable cause.
Any FAA or DoD change to how GPS interference tests are scheduled, announced, or located.
The outcome of the FCC proceeding on jamming near correctional facilities.
Published results from DIU's Transition of Quantum Sensing field tests.
DARPA RoQS sensors reaching their planned helicopter tests.

debate.intro: Two arguments run through this case: what the crash says about domestic testing, and what the real fix for GPS dependence is.

positions.heldBy: GPS Innovation Alliance (Lisa Dyer); Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.)
positions.argument: Jamming affects every receiver in range, not only the intended target. Tests are increasing, some have run without notice, and White Sands effects reach well beyond the range. Testing should move to larger areas, with better coordination.
positions.confidence: High that these are their positions

positions.heldBy: The rationale for expanded testing as reported by DefenseScoop; the Pentagon declined to comment
positions.argument: Forces have to train against counter-drone and electronic-warfare conditions they will face, and the FAA and DoD already coordinate windows through NOTAMs. In this case a NOTAM covered the area and controllers could pause the jamming on request.
positions.confidence: Medium: no named official has argued this publicly in this case

positions.heldBy: Implied by the GPS Innovation Alliance's recommendations
positions.argument: The fastest gains come from where and when tests run, how they are announced, and keeping crews proficient on ground-based approaches.
positions.confidence: Medium

positions.heldBy: Stated aims of DIU's Transition of Quantum Sensing and DARPA's RoQS; UK National Quantum Strategy
positions.argument: GPS will be jammed in any serious conflict regardless of domestic procedures. Platforms need navigation that does not rely on a radio signal at all, and quantum sensors are one of the few candidates that cannot be jammed in principle.
positions.confidence: High that this is the programs' rationale · Medium on timelines

debate.synthesis: Both fixes are needed and work on different clocks: procedures can change this year, while quantum backups are at field-trial stage.
debate.openQuestion: If the military has to jam GPS at home to prepare for war, and civilians share the same signal, who decides where readiness for war ends and peacetime safety takes priority, and on what evidence? And if quantum navigation succeeds, will civil aviation get it too, or will the gap between military and civilian resilience widen?

updates.text: GPS jamming around Schiphol affected at least seven aircraft (Dutch ministry); NRC reported 'dozens.' VRT, citing unnamed data experts, put it at about 80 aircraft over the Netherlands, Belgium, eastern England, and northwest Germany. Analyst J. Wiseman located a source north of Texel near three EU-sanctioned Russian ships in a navy-escorted convoy. There is no official attribution, and Belgium's Skeyes logged no reports.

Q-CTRL raised a $290 million Series C. Investors include In-Q-Tel, Lockheed Martin Ventures, EDGE Group (UAE), and Australia's National Reconstruction Fund. Q-CTRL already holds DARPA Robust Quantum Sensors awards (see key dates). 'Unjammable' is marketing language, and performance figures are company-reported.

UN News on a UNIDIR dialogue: UNIDIR cites a 500% rise in GPS spoofing in civil aviation from January to August 2024 and record maritime jamming in early 2026 during the Middle East crisis. A UN Security Council high-level meeting on emerging technology is scheduled for late November. No UN action yet.

entries.actor: Iran (IRGC-CEC / Shahid Kaveh, attributed by France)
entries.title: France Names an IRGC Unit for Sabotaging 700 Supermarket Cold Rooms
entries.bottomLine: France has publicly attributed an October 11–12 attack to Shahid Kaveh, a unit of the IRGC's electronic and cyber centre. The attack changed defrost settings on refrigeration controllers at about 700 retail sites, spoiling goods and causing at least 15 fires. France calls it the first offensive cyber campaign on its soil carried out purely for sabotage. It is the reverse of pre-positioning: the access was used, not held in reserve.
requires: Night of October 11–12, 2026: defrost settings on refrigeration controllers at about 700 French large-retail sites were changed to high temperatures. Goods were lost, and at least 15 sites had fires (ANSSI). The Foreign Ministry puts losses in the tens of millions of euros.

The same operation targeted Schneider Electric equipment at several small hydroelectric installations, with moderate effects. Some butcher shops, a slaughterhouse, and cooperative food plants were also reportedly affected (ANSSI).

Attribution (ANSSI, Nov. 9; Foreign Ministry, Nov. 10): France names the IRGC electronic and cyber centre (IRGC-CEC). It links the October attack to the Shahid Kaveh unit and earlier operations to the Shahid Shoostari unit. The stated evidence is infrastructure characteristics, signature tools, a propaganda outlet tied to Shahid Kaveh relaying the attack, and Persian-language traces in the attack infrastructure. ANSSI does not say how the attackers reached the controllers.

France ties earlier operations to the same centre: a 2023 defacement of Charlie Hebdo's online shop and theft of its data, and a 2024 intrusion into a company that runs display kiosks. The 2024 attackers tried to show doctored images about Israeli athletes during the Paris Olympics and were caught before the images appeared.

Response: France summoned Iran's ambassador. The Paris prosecutor opened a judicial investigation and requested international arrest warrants for several Shahid Kaveh members, and France proposed further EU sanctions. The technical report is CERTFR-2026-CTI-009.

keyDates.label: Overnight sabotage of about 700 retail refrigeration sites and small hydro equipment

strategicRead.head: Pre-positioning, then use.
strategicRead.body: CISA's Volt Typhoon advisories describe access held for a future crisis. This is the other half of that model: in peacetime, on one night and at national scale, the attackers used their access to refrigeration and small-hydro controllers against civilian commerce.

strategicRead.head: Low-value targets, high-volume effect.
strategicRead.body: No single supermarket cold room matters strategically. Seven hundred at once, plus small hydro sites, shows that widely deployed, lightly defended operational technology can be hit in bulk. Private firms bear the cost, and the state receives the message.

strategicRead.head: Naming the unit, not just the state.
strategicRead.body: France named a specific unit within a month, listed its evidence categories, and sought arrest warrants. Naming units and individuals is meant to make people carry a cost, not only Iran.

indicators: EU sanctions listings published in the Official Journal
Arrest warrants issued or circulated internationally for Shahid Kaveh members
Similar refrigeration or building-automation sabotage in other EU states
Iranian retaliation or further denial statements
Any government attribution of U.S. cold-chain incidents (none so far)

debate.intro: The open argument is what any response can achieve against a state that denies the attack.

positions.heldBy: French government (Foreign Ministry statement); EU High Representative Kaja Kallas (Nov. 16)
positions.argument: Public attribution, arrest warrants, and EU listings raise the cost for the unit and its members. They signal that sabotage on EU soil will be answered collectively, and they build a record for later measures.
positions.confidence: High that this is their position

positions.heldBy: CISA and partner agencies' cold-chain alert (Nov. 5; no actor named)
positions.argument: Officers who never travel are not stopped by indictments. Removing internet exposure and default access from controllers prevents the next attack whoever launches it.
positions.confidence: Medium: the U.S. alert does not discuss France or Iran

debate.synthesis: The two approaches are complementary. The disagreement is over how much punishment can deter when the defender is a supermarket chain.
debate.openQuestion: If a state can spoil a country's food supply for a night and the strongest available answer is an EU sanctions listing, at what point does sabotage of civilian infrastructure become a use of force? One view holds that no cyber effect without casualties crosses that line. Another holds that a deliberate pattern of harm to civilian infrastructure should cross it even without deaths. Where should the line be, and who decides?

updates.text: At the EU Foreign Affairs Council, High Representative Kallas said the EU is preparing further sanctions on Iran, citing the attacks on France. France's foreign minister called for listings. Nothing had been adopted as of Nov. 23. Iran denies involvement.

Separate U.S. context, which no government has linked to Iran: CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, and DOT jointly urged critical-infrastructure operators to secure industrial refrigeration and cold-chain controllers. No actor named.

France's blood service (EFS) confirmed that three of its cold rooms were affected through a vendor on Nov. 3–4 (Le Quotidien du Médecin). The incident is unattributed, and France has not linked it to Shahid Kaveh.

entries.actor: CISA (commissioned); AdaptiveMobile Security and Telecom Defense (authors)
entries.title: The SS7 Warning, Four Years Early: CISA's Withheld Telecom Report
entries.bottomLine: A June 2022 report prepared for CISA found that U.S. phone-network signaling allows location tracking and interception by anyone who can rent access to it, and called the U.S. the most targeted country in the world. It became public, redacted, only in October 2026 through an EPIC FOIA lawsuit, two years after Salt Typhoon. The structural point: the signaling layer still trusts any network that pays to join it.
requires: The document is the 'U.S. Telecommunications Insecurity Report' (June 2022), prepared for CISA under a DHS Science and Technology contract by AdaptiveMobile Security with Telecom Defense. It is marked preliminary and not a coordinated DHS position. EPIC obtained it in redacted form through a FOIA lawsuit (release dated Oct. 29, 2026; reported by Bloomberg Nov. 19).

Findings: SS7 was designed around mutual trust, with no firewalling. Signaling messages can reveal a target's network, device identifiers, and real-time location. Many U.S. operators screen domestic SS7 and Diameter traffic less than international traffic, and national roaming multiplies the entry points. A few signaling aggregators carry much of U.S. operators' traffic. Leasing of Global Titles (signaling network addresses) to third parties lacks oversight. 5G non-standalone networks carry the legacy exposure forward.

Observed activity (March–May 2022): location and routing queries against U.S. subscribers, and more than 9,000 'Global Opcode' violations between May 4 and 11, over 2,000 of them within a single 24-hour period.

The report says the U.S. 'remains the most targeted country in the world' for signaling exploits. It traced traffic to Global Titles leased through brokers in central and southern Europe and assessed that such brokers likely act as proxies for nation-state actors. Most of its policy recommendations are redacted.

Bloomberg cites unnamed former officials saying Salt Typhoon used SS7 for reconnaissance only. CTIA, the wireless industry group, says SS7 is not used in 4G or 5G. Neither claim comes from the report.

keyDates.label: June 2022: report delivered under CISA contract (month only)

strategicRead.head: The weakness is a business model, not a bug.
strategicRead.body: Signaling access is for sale: Global Titles are leased, and aggregators resell connectivity. A state service does not need to hack a carrier to query it; it needs a front company with a lease. That is why the report's fixes are regulatory, such as oversight of leasing and review of ownership, as much as technical.

strategicRead.head: Intercept capability is attack surface.
strategicRead.body: Salt Typhoon reached lawful-intercept systems. This report shows the signaling layer was already open. Together they suggest that every access path built into a network, legal or legacy, is a target.

strategicRead.head: What changed since 2022 cannot be judged from this release.
strategicRead.body: The useful question is not why the report was withheld but which of its recommendations were adopted. The redactions cover most of the policy section.

debate.intro: The argument is over who should close the signaling gap.

positions.heldBy: The report's authors (2022 recommendations, as far as unredacted)
positions.argument: Carriers have had more than a decade of public SS7 research and still screen domestic traffic lightly. Oversight of Global Title leasing, continuously updated filtering, and review of ownership and vendors need a regulator behind them.
positions.confidence: High on the unredacted recommendations

positions.heldBy: CTIA (as reported by Bloomberg)
positions.argument: SS7 is a legacy protocol not used in 4G and 5G. Firewalls and the move to newer network cores address the risk without new rules.
positions.confidence: Medium: a reported statement; the report says non-standalone 5G still carries legacy exposure

debate.synthesis: Both sides agree SS7 is legacy. They disagree on whether legacy means retired or still exposed.
debate.openQuestion: If foreign services can rent their way into the U.S. phone network, is signaling security a consumer-protection problem, a counterintelligence problem, or a national-defense problem? The answer decides whether the FCC, CISA, or nobody fixes it.

updates.text: Canada's Senate national security committee heard Signal, Meta, Tailscale, and Citizen Lab on Bill C-22 (Lawful Access Act). The bill would let ministers order providers to build intercept capability and would allow metadata retention of up to six months. It passed the House on June 18 and is not yet law.

Enea reported 'SilentAir': a state-level actor (Enea's assessment, high confidence) abusing SS7 and Diameter over IPX through compromised operator equipment to divert calls and SMS, mainly of Taiwanese VIPs, including interception of two-factor codes. Enea rates a China link Low. This is vendor reporting with no government corroboration. Enea's AdaptiveMobile unit co-wrote the 2022 report.
Check Point reported a China-nexus framework, 'CopperDragon', at three or more Latin American telecoms and called any link to Salt Typhoon 'unclear'. This is vendor reporting only.

entries.title: DeepMind's Agents Verify Signal's Code, Not Just Its Design
entries.bottomLine: Google DeepMind says AI agents proved key security properties of the compiled code behind the Signal protocol in about four weeks. Humans wrote and reviewed the specification, and the Lean proof checker verified the proofs. If the result holds up, proving that cryptographic code does what its designers intended just became much cheaper. That matters most for the post-quantum migration, where implementation bugs are a bigger near-term risk than broken math.
requires: Announced Nov. 10, 2026, together with the AlphaProof Code framework and a technical paper. The verification artifacts are open source. DeepMind calls this the first formal verification of a widely deployed protocol's implementation by any method, with or without AI.

Method: humans and models translated Signal's security goals into formal specifications, and experts reviewed each one. Agents running on Gemini Carbon wrote the proofs in Lean, more than six million lines according to the blog post (another DeepMind summary says three million). About 1% of the code was flagged for human review, and the Lean checker verified the rest.
Test: the team reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated copy of the code. Both times, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.

Scope: the blog post gives one example property (messages stay protected before and after a temporary device compromise). It does not list which libsignal components or protocol stages were covered, or state its cryptographic assumptions. Proofs about an implementation normally assume the underlying primitives are secure. Coverage notes that the guarantees apply to the library, not the Signal apps (The Next Web).
Signal's CTO, Ehren Kret, said the verification gives Signal greater confidence in its code's privacy guarantees.

keyDates.label: DeepMind announces AlphaProof Code and the Signal verification

strategicRead.head: Correct math, wrong code.
strategicRead.body: Most real-world cryptographic failures come from implementations, not broken algorithms. Proving that code matches its specification targets the layer where breaches actually happen.

strategicRead.head: It matters for the migration.
strategicRead.body: Every organization moving to ML-KEM and ML-DSA under CNSA 2.0 and NIST IR 8547 is shipping new cryptographic code on a deadline. Cheap, machine-checked proofs of that code would lower the risk that the migration itself introduces flaws.

strategicRead.head: The same tool finds holes.
strategicRead.body: The bug test showed the system can also prove code insecure. A tool that searches for proofs of insecurity is a vulnerability-research tool, and its value depends on who runs it first.

indicators: Independent review of the paper and the released proof artifacts
Extension to other protocols (TLS, MLS) or to post-quantum libraries
NSA or NIST references to machine-checked proofs in validation or CNSA 2.0 guidance
Bugs found in deployed cryptographic libraries through this method

debate.intro: The argument is over what 'verified' should be allowed to mean.

positions.heldBy: Google DeepMind; Signal (CTO statement)
positions.argument: The proofs reach compiled code, a trusted kernel checks them, and they caught reintroduced bugs. Work that took expert teams years took weeks.
positions.confidence: High that this is their position

positions.position: Verified against a specification, under assumptions
positions.heldBy: Standard formal-methods caution; skeptical press coverage
positions.argument: A proof is only as good as its specification. Properties left out of the specification, and primitives assumed to be perfect, fall outside the guarantee. 'Signal is proven secure' overstates the result.
positions.confidence: High on the principle · Medium on how much it limits this result, since the full scope is in the paper

debate.synthesis: Both are true. The result moves the bottleneck from writing proofs to writing the right specification.
debate.openQuestion: If AI makes it cheap to prove code secure, it also makes it cheap to prove code insecure. Does verification at machine speed favor defenders, who can verify before shipping, or attackers, who need only one gap in the specification? And once proofs take weeks rather than years, should governments require them for the cryptography in national security systems?

entries.actor: Unattributed operator (Russian-language artifacts); PRC-, DPRK-, and Iran-nexus actors (GTIG)
entries.title: Google: Attackers Now Turn Patches Into Exploits Without a Human
entries.bottomLine: Google's Threat Intelligence Group reports the first case it has seen of attackers fully automating the path from a published patch to a working exploit, with no human in the loop. The operator is unattributed. The strategic effect is on time: the gap between a fix being published and being exploited is shrinking toward the pace of machines rather than people.
requires: Source: GTIG AI Threat Tracker, 'Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold' (Nov. 16, 2026), produced with Mandiant.

exploit_agent is a multi-agent framework GTIG found on an exposed staging server, connected to multiple frontier and locally hosted language models. It continuously compares popular web-application code before and after patch announcements, identifies likely vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and executes them. Its post-compromise scripts handled reconnaissance, brute-forcing, and webshells. Telemetry suggests interest in French media, entertainment, and education websites. No actor is attributed; an environment file contained Russian-language comments about API keys for 'auto-exploitation.'

CAIRN, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework, was observed in intrusions that included targets in the U.S. aerospace sector. The report does not attribute that activity to a country.

DPRK: a suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE cluster used fake recruiter profiles, whose images carried Google's SynthID watermark, to reach cryptocurrency firms in North America and Europe. After getting in, it edited Claude Code settings files in internal repositories so that starting the tool downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor.

In Q3 2026, PRC-nexus actors used language models for reconnaissance and exploit weaponization, and GTIG has evidence that one PRC-nexus group was building its own automated attack framework, likely for espionage. Iran's CALANQUE ION (formerly APT42) uses models, including Gemini, for reconnaissance and social engineering.
GTIG counts zero-day exploits rising from a 2025 average of 8 per month to 11 per month in 2026, with 22 in August.

keyDates.label: August 2026: 22 zero-days exploited in one month (GTIG count)
GTIG AI Threat Tracker published

strategicRead.head: Speed, not sophistication.
strategicRead.body: exploit_agent went after known, already patched flaws. What changed is how quickly an n-day becomes a working attack. Defenses built around monthly patch cycles assume an attacker working at human pace.

strategicRead.head: Noisy now, quieter later.
strategicRead.body: GTIG assesses that current frameworks trade stealth for speed and leave forensic traces, so stealth-focused state services are less likely to rely on them in targeted environments for now. Cybercriminals, who care less about stealth, will keep adopting them (GTIG, high confidence).

strategicRead.head: The developer toolchain is the new perimeter.
strategicRead.body: The DPRK case used an AI coding tool's own configuration to deliver malware, after the same fake-recruiter approach seen in the Binance theft. AI agent tooling inside developer environments is now a way in.

indicators: A government attribution of an exploit_agent-style framework to a state actor
CISA guidance shortening remediation deadlines for known exploited vulnerabilities
Published time-to-exploit measurements after patch releases
Further abuse of AI coding-agent configuration files
Vendors moving to automatic patching for internet-facing software

debate.intro: The debate is whether autonomy changes the balance between attack and defense or only the tempo.

positions.heldBy: GTIG (Nov. 16 report)
positions.argument: Attackers need one working exploit, while defenders must patch everything. Automation compresses the attacker's side of the race fastest, and the frameworks are open source.
positions.confidence: High that this is GTIG's framing

positions.heldBy: Google (Big Sleep, CodeMender); DeepMind's code-verification work
positions.argument: The same models can find and fix flaws before release and verify code formally. If defenders automate discovery and patch deployment, the window shrinks for both sides.
positions.confidence: Medium: a company's position about its own products

debate.synthesis: Both sides are automating. What differs is who must still wait for human approval.
debate.openQuestion: If defending at machine speed means letting AI patch production systems without a human sign-off, who accepts the risk of a bad automatic fix? In military networks, where one change can affect a weapon or communications system, is human-speed defense a safety requirement or a vulnerability?

entries.title: Anduril in the Cryptologic Stack: Cyber Effects, a Quantum Pilot, and a PQC Hiring Push
entries.bottomLine: Anduril is best known for drones and counter-drone systems, but its public record now reaches into this site's subjects: cyber and RF effects running inside its Lattice command-and-control software, a quantum optimization pilot for missile-defense planning, and job postings for post-quantum and CNSA 2.0 certification work. None of this month's AI and quantum headlines involve Anduril directly. The link is that a C2 vendor running cyber effects at the tactical edge inherits every trend in exploit speed, code verification, and cryptographic migration.
requires: DoD link (this track's criterion): on March 13, 2026, the Army awarded Anduril a 10-year enterprise IDIQ contract with a ceiling of up to $20 billion. It consolidates more than 120 separate procurement actions for Anduril's commercial technology, including the Lattice suite. The figure is a ceiling, not obligated funds.

Cyber and RF effects: on May 18, 2026, Booz Allen and Anduril announced that three Booz Allen products run on Anduril's Menace compute and communications systems, integrated with Lattice: the Sit(x) coordination layer, the Dynamic Effects Tasking System for tasking cyber and RF effects, and Zero Trust controls. The integration was demonstrated at SOF Week 2026.

Quantum: on Jan. 27, 2026, D-Wave, Davidson Technologies, and Anduril reported a proof of concept applying quantum-classical hybrid optimization to air and missile defense planning. They claimed at least 10x faster time-to-solution and 45–60 additional intercepts in a 500-missile simulation (company-reported, not independently verified). D-Wave's annealing systems cannot run Shor's algorithm. Anduril Labs also lists a quantum software role covering both annealing and gate-model platforms.

Cryptography: Anduril job postings from September 2026 ask for CNSA 2.0 or post-quantum migration experience alongside vulnerability research and exploit development. Another posting seeks a senior engineer to take Anduril's cryptographic services through U.S. government validation and certification, requiring post-quantum experience.

keyDates.label: D-Wave, Davidson, and Anduril missile-defense optimization proof of concept
Army enterprise contract, ceiling up to $20 billion
Booz Allen cyber, RF effects, and Zero Trust integrated on Menace and Lattice

strategicRead.head: Integration is the product.
strategicRead.body: The Booz Allen integration puts situational awareness, cyber and RF tasking, and security controls into one deployable system. That shortens the path from finding a target to acting on it, and it concentrates risk: one compromised node now touches all three.

strategicRead.head: The PQC deadline reaches vendors.
strategicRead.body: Equipment sold into national security systems must support CNSA 2.0 algorithms on CNSSP 15's timeline. Hiring for validation and post-quantum migration is what that requirement looks like inside a contractor.

strategicRead.head: Quantum optimization is a hedge, not a capability.
strategicRead.body: Annealing for planning problems is commercially available, but its advantage over the best classical methods is disputed. The defense-relevant performance claim is company-reported.

strategicRead.head: Why this month's news reaches Anduril.
strategicRead.body: GTIG's automated patch-to-exploit pipeline, DeepMind's code verification, and NVIDIA's faster error-correction research all sit upstream of any vendor fielding networked C2: faster attacks, cheaper assurance, and a moving quantum timeline.
strategicRead.confidence: Low (analyst linkage; no source connects them to Anduril)

indicators: Accreditation of Lattice or Menace cyber-effects capabilities for additional networks or services
The D-Wave pilot moving to a government-funded contract
Anduril products appearing in NIST CMVP or NSA validation listings with post-quantum algorithms
Any public security incident or disclosed vulnerability involving Lattice

debate.intro: This track asks the same question of every firm: is it building something the government cannot build itself?

positions.axis: Should cyber effects live inside vendor C2 platforms?
positions.heldBy: Booz Allen and Anduril (May 18 release)
positions.argument: Operators should identify, task, and act on targets in one system instead of switching between tools, and one integrated system is simpler to accredit.
positions.confidence: High that this is their position

positions.axis: Should cyber effects live inside vendor C2 platforms?
positions.heldBy: General zero-trust and supply-chain security principle; no named critic of this integration
positions.argument: Putting effects, C2, and security controls on one vendor's stack makes that stack a single high-value target and deepens dependence on one company's software.
positions.confidence: Low: no named holder of this position on this deal

debate.synthesis: Speed and concentration come from the same design choice. The question is whether verification and accreditation keep pace with the integration.
debate.openQuestion: When a venture-backed company's software both sees the battlefield and tasks cyber effects, does the government still own the decision chain, or does it rent it? And if a vendor's code becomes the C2 layer, who verifies that code, and how?
